system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 5 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2183-11-27 03:29:00 to 2183-12-01 18:17:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old woman with a complex history including fibrosing mesenteritis, multiple abdominal surgeries, chronic TPN dependence, and recurrent line infections was admitted due to a positive blood culture for coagulase-negative staphylococcus from her PICC line. She remained clinically stable without fever or systemic signs of infection. The PICC line was removed, and subsequent cultures from the line tip and repeated blood draws were negative. Multiple attempts to place a new upper extremity central line failed due to venous stenoses and a non-occlusive thrombus in the right subclavian vein. A tunneled left femoral double-lumen central line was successfully placed for ongoing TPN. Infectious disease recommended further molecular testing to evaluate for a persistent source. The patient was discharged home with home health services to manage her line and nutrition, with follow-up arranged with her ID and GI specialists.
problems: Other and unspecified infection due to central venous catheter
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ female with fibrosing mesenteritis, new right chest
pain and tachycardia.

___.

TECHNIQUE:  Helical MDCT images were acquired through the chest without and
with intravenous contrast, per the chest CTA protocol.  5- and 2.5-mm axial,
5-mm coronal and sagittal, and 3 mm bilateral oblique multiplanar reformats
were generated.

FINDINGS:  There is no main, branch, lobar, or segmental pulmonary embolus. 
The main pulmonary artery is enlarged at 3.5 cm, indicative of pulmonary
arterial hypertension.  The thoracic aorta is normal in caliber throughout. 
Heart is normal in size, with leftward bowing of the interventricular septum,
indicative of right heart strain.  Calcifications are noted in the left
anterior descending coronary artery.

The left brachiocephalic vein is chronically attenuated, with numerous left
chest wall and mediastinal venous collaterals, the majority of which drain
into the azygos vein.  

Sub-1-mm pulmonary nodules are present in the right upper lobe (2:19).  There
is no focal consolidation.  No pleural effusions are present.  Central airways
are patent to the subsegmental levels.

A prominent axillary node measures 7 mm in short axis, but demonstrates a
fatty hilum.  Mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes are not pathologically
enlarged.

Note is made of a small hiatal hernia.

Evaluation is not tailored for subdiaphragmatic evaluation, but reveals fatty
infiltration of the liver and chronic postoperative pneumobilia.

There is a mildly displaced fracture of the right anterior fifth rib.  Callus
formation is present, indicating subacute injury.  Nerve stimulator device is
present within the posterior spinal canal, spanning the T4-T8 levels. 
Abandoned lead is present in the right posterior soft tissues.

IMPRESSION:
1.  No PE.
2.  Subacute anterior fifth rib fracture.
3.  Pulmonary arterial hypertension.
4.  Chronic left brachiocephalic vein occlusion.
5.  Fatty liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were brought in with right-sided chest pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started yesterday morning. It’s sharp and gets worse when I breathe deeply or move. It’s been getting stronger since then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever, cough, or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fever or trouble breathing. Just the pain and this ongoing nausea I’ve had for weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history and the pain, we did a CT scan of your chest to check for blood clots or fractures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Was anything found?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—no blood clot in your lungs. But we did find a small fracture in your fifth rib on the right side, near the front. It looks a few days old.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A rib fracture? But I didn’t fall or get hit. Could it be from vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s very possible. Severe or repeated vomiting can strain the chest muscles and even cause rib fractures. That might explain why the pain is higher than the fracture site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve been vomiting a lot lately. What about my line? Should we be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We drew blood from your femoral tunneled line, and the culture came back positive for Enterococcus avium, a type of bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no—not another line infection. Do I need it removed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We consulted Infectious Disease. They don’t think removal is necessary this time. We’ll treat it with antibiotics and a special lock solution in the line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What kind of antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting daptomycin, given through your line once a day. It covers this type of bacteria well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the lock solution?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Originally, we planned to use ethanol, but there’s a shortage. So we’ll use vancomycin instead—put in the line for two hours before each TPN session.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can manage that at home with help. Will I need this for long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll go home on daptomycin for 10 more days. A nurse will come to give it daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my pain? Morphine helps a little, but not enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adding Toradol, an anti-inflammatory, to help with the rib and muscle pain. But we’ll only use it short-term because of your stomach issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s smart. I’ve had gastritis before. What about my TPN? My G-tube output has been high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your GI doctor thinks the high output suggests a partial blockage. We’ve restarted TPN to support your nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll need that at home too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, same as before—through your femoral line. We’ll coordinate home care for TPN, antibiotics, and the vancomycin locks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat blood cultures are all negative—no bacteria growing from your IV or line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! Does that mean the infection is clearing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a good sign. The single positive culture likely came from the line. With treatment, we expect it to resolve fully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You rated it 5 out of 10 this morning—down from 8. The Toradol seems to be helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. But I’ve been a bit nauseous since starting it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We expected that. We’ll stop Toradol today and rely more on morphine. We don’t want to risk stomach irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s fine. What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most are continuing as before. We adjusted gabapentin and lamotrigine doses slightly based on your weight and kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show stable kidney function and mild anemia, which you’ve had before. White count is normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any update on the bacteria?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The final sensitivity report shows the Enterococcus is sensitive to daptomycin, vancomycin, and ampicillin. We’re confident in your treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I feel better already. Pain is down to a 3.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent progress. We’ll keep monitoring, but you’re on track for discharge in a couple of days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your repeat blood cultures remain negative. Infectious Disease confirms you can finish daptomycin at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the vancomycin lock?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue that before each TPN session. A nurse will show your caregiver how to do it safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see Infectious Disease in one week. Also, get blood work—CBC, basic metabolic panel, and CK—before that visit and fax the results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my abdominal pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s still present but at your usual level. We didn’t find any new obstruction or acute issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared for discharge today. You’ve improved significantly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue daptomycin daily for 10 days, use vancomycin lock before TPN, take your regular meds, and monitor for fever or redness at the line site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the pain gets worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use your morphine as needed. Most rib fractures heal in 4–6 weeks with rest and pain control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I feel much more comfortable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. The home health team will arrive before noon to set everything up. We’ll also send your records to your specialists.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes. We’re here to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your discharge summary mentions the rib fracture and line infection as main issues. All other conditions are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I read it. Everything looks accurate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. The nurse will go over your meds one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready whenever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have you out within the hour. Rest well at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Just keep up with the plan and follow up as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, and feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. See you in follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old woman with a complex medical history including fibrosing mesenteritis, chronic TPN dependence via a tunneled femoral catheter, and recurrent line infections was admitted for right-sided chest pain. Imaging revealed a subacute anterior fifth rib fracture, likely due to prolonged vomiting, and a blood culture from her femoral line grew Enterococcus avium. She was treated with intravenous daptomycin and vancomycin antibiotic locks in the catheter, with no need for line removal per Infectious Disease. Pain improved with a short course of Toradol, later discontinued due to GI concerns, and she was transitioned back to morphine. Repeat blood cultures remained negative, and she was discharged home with home health services to complete a 10-day course of daptomycin, continue TPN, and perform vancomycin locks. Follow-up was arranged with Infectious Disease and primary care.
